title: Two truths
hookLine: Nagarjuna: a conventional truth for everyday life, an ultimate truth of emptiness
carry: a snake picked up by the wrong end

cards: A wooden chair stands by the door. Sit on it and it's plainly a chair: it holds your weight, it scrapes the floor, and if a leg cracks, you fall. Now look a second way.
The chair is a tree that grew in rain and sun, a carpenter's hands, glue, nails, and a shape someone named chair. Take those away and no chair is left hiding underneath. Both looks are true.
One gets you through the day; the other goes deeper. Nagarjuna had a name for holding both.

teach.h: THE BUDDHAS TEACH BY TWO TRUTHS.
teach.b: In his Root Verses on the Middle Way, Nagarjuna says the Buddhas teach the Dharma by relying on two truths. One is conventional truth, the world as we use it every day.

teach.h: ULTIMATE: NOTHING STANDS ON ITS OWN.
teach.b: The other is ultimate truth, and for Nagarjuna the ultimate is emptiness: nothing exists on its own, from its own side, apart from causes and names. The chair is empty of a separate chair-self.
That doesn't make it nothing. It still holds you up. Why keep both?

The verses go on: without relying on the everyday, the ultimate can't be taught, and without understanding the ultimate, nirvana isn't reached. So the everyday truth isn't a lie to throw away. It's the ladder.
Words, names, kindness, rules for monks, the teaching itself all live in conventional truth, and they're how anyone gets near the ultimate. Then, in the same chapter, a warning.

teach.h: A SNAKE HELD BY THE WRONG END.
teach.b: Emptiness wrongly grasped is dangerous, like a snake picked up by the wrong end. Someone who hears that everything is empty and decides nothing matters has grabbed the tail.

Buddhist schools read the two truths in more than one way. Tibetan teachers in the Madhyamaka tradition have argued carefully over exactly how the two fit together, and Theravada teachers use a related pair of their own.

teach.h: ONE WORLD, TWO WAYS OF SEEING.
teach.b: In Nagarjuna's verses, the shape is this: one world, two ways of seeing it, and the teaching leans on both.

how: Students in Tibetan monasteries and Mahayana study programs learn the two truths as a core topic of Madhyamaka philosophy, often by memorizing Nagarjuna's verses and debating how the two truths relate.

games.q: a student hears that everything is empty and says, "then nothing matters, so why keep any rules?" you're the teacher. what do you say?
o: "emptiness held wrongly bites, like a snake held by the tail."
games.why: Nagarjuna's own warning: emptiness misunderstood harms the one who grasps it. the everyday truth still matters.

practice: Choose something within reach, a pen or your own hand, and first let it simply be what it is: name it, and notice what it does for you.

Then look the second way, tracing what it's made of, who made it and what it depends on, until no single thing is left standing on its own. Go back and forth slowly with the breath, and let it be a pen again.

wordCard.voice: Two truths. Conventional truth for the everyday world, and ultimate truth, emptiness, as Nagarjuna teaches it. Without the first, the second cannot be taught. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit paramartha: the ultimate, the highest meaning, one of the two truths.

carryVoice: Your line: a snake picked up by the wrong end. Emptiness, held well, never makes the day stop mattering. Day nine hundred fifty-seven, done.

sources.ref: Mulamadhyamakakarika 24.11 (emptiness wrongly seen, like a snake wrongly grasped)
